messages.subject_clean: Using temperature as a time varying session-specific covariate
messages.body_plain:
Dear SECR users,

I would like to pick up on the issue of Chris concerning the addition of time varying covariates differing among sessions in multisession models. As Chris, I would like to explore the effect of the temperature, as time varying covariate, on the estimation of demographic parameters of three stream-dwelling newt populations (i.e. three sessions, spatially independant). I am using secrlinear package (secr 4.3.3).
I have 3 or 4 occasions per session, all realized during the activity period of the species. Each session has its own detector layout.
I used the method proposed by Murray to construct a list of time varying covariates but I have some troubles when fitting the model.

Here is my process:

# list of time covariates
multi_tcov_2019 <- list('cassrats' = c(NA,cassrats_tcov[1:3,3]),
                        'Fougax' = c(fougax_tcov[12:15,3]),
                        'Salau' = c(NA,NA,salau_tcov[5:6,3]))

timevaryingcov(multi_tcov_2019$cassrats)<- list(blockt = 1:4)
timevaryingcov(multi_tcov_2019$Fougax)<- list(blockt = 1:4)
timevaryingcov(multi_tcov_2019$Salau)<- list(blockt = 1:4)

# output (there is some occasions with NA in two sessions)
> multi_tcov_2019
$`cassrats` [1] NA 10.6505 12.1100 14.7090
attr(,"timevaryingcov")
attr(,"timevaryingcov")$`blockt`
[1] 1 2 3 4

$Fougax [1] 14.9475 16.8080 15.1865 12.8830
attr(,"timevaryingcov")
attr(,"timevaryingcov")$`blockt`
[1] 1 2 3 4

$Salau [1] NA 18.616 15.091 NA
attr(,"timevaryingcov")
attr(,"timevaryingcov")$`blockt`
[1] 1 2 3 4

# fit the model
fitmulti_2019_11 <- secr.fit(casper2019_multi_tous, mask = list(cassratsstreammask, fougaxstreammask, salaustreammask), trace = FALSE,
                             model = list(g0~tcov+session), hcov = "Sex",
                             timecov = multi_tcov_2019,
                             details = list(userdist = networkdistance))

Warning messages:
1: In secr.design.MS <http://secr.design.MS>(capthist, model, timecov, sessioncov, groups, :   # I supposed this is due to the NAs in short sessions
length of 'timecov' exceeds number of occasions
2: In secr.design.MS <http://secr.design.MS>(capthist, model, timecov, sessioncov, groups, :
length of 'timecov' exceeds number of occasions
3: In secr.fit(casper2019_multi_tous, mask = list(cassratsstreammask, :   at least one variance calculation failed

# output of the predictions

When I check the predictions of my model, there is no predictions for the different levels of my time variable but only for 0° (while I don't have any 0° in the time varying datasets).

I would really appreciate any advice or assistance!
Let me know if more detail is needed.

Thanks in advance
Manon

>
> For multisession data in which time covariates differ among sessions it should work to provide timecov as an R list in which each component is the vector of time covariates (temperatures) for one session. This should be documented somewhere! Testing it I discovered a bug that causes an error if the number of occasions per session varies, but there is an easy workaround (pad the covariate vector for short sessions with NA).

> >
> > fit_Jan18<-secr.fit(Jan18, start = list(D=1000, g0 = 0.01, sigma = 1), model = D ~session, buffer = 10, detectfn = 'HN', trace = FALSE)

> > fit_Nov18<-secr.fit(Nov18, start = list(D=1000, g0 = 0.01, sigma = 1), model = D ~session, buffer = 10, detectfn = 'HN', trace = FALSE)
> >
> >
> >
> > fit_Nov17<-summary(fit_Nov17)
> >
> > fit_Jan18<-summary(fit_Jan18)
> >
> > fit_Nov18<-summary(fit_Nov18)
> >
> >
> > I'm keen to use a model selection approach to see how daily temperature and behavioural responses to capture affect model fit. However, my current difficulty is how to include temperature as a covariate that varies by occasion. I understand this can be done using timecov() ....
> >
> >
> >
> > ## something like...
> >
> > fit_Nov17<-secr.fit(Nov17, start = list(D=1000, g0 = 0.01, sigma = 1), model = list(D~session, g0~tcov), buffer = 10, detectfn = 'HN', trace = FALSE, timecov = c(21.2, 19.3, 20.0, 21.1, 20.9, 19.4, 20.7))
> >
> >
> >
> > .... however, as the trapping grids ('sessions') are spread across two cities (and therefore were not in use simultaneously) I'd like the temperatures to be specific to the session as well as varying with time. Is this possible or would it be best to model the trapping periods of each city separately (this would greatly reduce my already small sample size)?
> >
> >
> > Any advice or assistance would be greatly appreciated. Please let me know if more detail is needed to understand the problem.
> >
> >
> > Many thanks
> >
> > Chris

1) These are different models - the lapply() approach ensures all parameters are estimated independently for each session. The other approach forces shared estimates of the detection parameters. And the density estimates are really not that different if you look at the CI.
2) Your 'covariatesource' has a column labelled 'V3' not 'Habitat' (this is a quirk of how read.mask works). You can fix this with
names(covariates(covariatesource)) <- 'Habitat'
Better still, recognise that habitat varies at the session level and use a session covariate instead of a mask covariate. Then

sessionhab <- data.frame(habitat = c('Rainforest', 'DrySclerophyll', 'Rainforest', 'DrySclerophyll')) # matching sessions 1-4
fitted2 <- secr.fit(PossumCH, mask = masks, detectfn = 'HN',
    model = D~habitat, sessioncov = sessionhab, trace = FALSE, verify = FALSE)
predict(fitted, newdata = data.frame(habitat = factor(c('DrySclerophyll', 'Rainforest'))))

Hello !

I have to estimate the density of roe deer by SCR in the east of Mavrovo National Park in Macedonia. First some details about the survey design. Considering the size of the home range of a roe deer (0,5 – 1 km²) (Morellet et al., 2013) a 1-km² grid cells was overlaid and two cells similar in their ruggedness and forest cover (Zimmermann, pers. comm.) were selected. Twelve camera traps were distributed in each cell, looking for roe deer signs (like day beds, paths or vegetation damages) in order to increase capture probability. However, one camera wasn’t found at the end of the survey so footages from 23 cameras were used in total.

So I have several outstanding issues, here are the first ones.

1/ AIC or AICc?

I found that the ratio between the sample size and the number of parameters must be greater than 40 (Burnham & Anderson, 2002) in order to use AIC. But two queries, the number of parameters varies depending on the model used and I don’t know if the sample size concerns the number of individuals detected or the number of independent encounter events. Depending on which one I choose, the best models are not at all the same. Here a shortened summary :

detectors used    23 23 23 23 23 23 23 23 23 23 23 23 23 23  1403

 2/ Buffer width

I am lost in all the possibilities to choose the buffer width (rule of thumb of 4*RSPV, suggest.buffer, mask.checks, esa.plots, secr.fit) a priori or a posteriori.

Here the results a priori :

> 4*RPSV(capturedata, CC = TRUE)
[1] 1229.677

> suggest.buffer(capturedata, detectfn = 'HN', RBtarget = 0.001)
[1] 1425

Results a posteriori :
> SCR.naive = secr.fit(capturedata, buffer = 1300, trace = FALSE)
#No errors or warnings

> esa.plot(SCR.naive, max.buffer = 10*RPSV(capturedata, CC = TRUE), cex.lab = 1.2)
> abline(v = c(rot.buffer, suggested.buffer), lty = c(3,5), col = 'black')
> abline(v = 1300, col = 'red')
#esa.plot output in attached file

> suggest.buffer(SCR.naive)
[1] 1934

So what now ? mask.check function ? But what is your criterion for choosing the buffer width? Likelihood or density? Buffer from which density no longer varies at all or for the lowest likelihood?

3/ Detection function

When should I choose it? before or after the construction of the mask?

Thank you in advance, at least for the time you will take to read my post!

messages.body_plain:
I am attempting to run a multisession model for a rabbit population with 2 sessions and 2 occasions per session (population was surveyed twice in 2018 and twice in 2019). My input is a capt file that includes data from both years, a list of trap files (one for each year), and a list of masks (one for each year, because I am running this for a metapopulation, and some sites were not surveyed in both years so the masks differ slightly by year).

First I tried the following code, but the output for session 1 and session 2 was exactly the same, when I was expecting different estimates by year:

captures1819<- read.table("capeelizCapt.txt")

#create trapfile
trapfile18<- read.traps("capeeliz_proxtrap_18.txt", detector = "proximity")
trapfile19<- read.traps("capeeliz_proxtrap_19.txt", detector = "proximity")
trapfile<-list(trapfile18,trapfile19)

#2018mask
mask1<- read.mask(file = "capeeliz18_mask.txt", spacing = 30)
#2019mask
mask2<- read.mask(file = "capeeliz19_mask.txt", spacing = 30)
#metapop1819mask
mask <-list(mask1,mask2)

CHmetapop <-make.capthist(captures1819, trapfile,
                          fmt = "XY", noccasions = 2, tol = 3, snapXY = TRUE)

summary(CHmetapop, terse=TRUE)
verify(CHmetapop, report = 2)

metapop.fit <- secr.fit (CHmetapop, model = list(D~1, g0~1, sigma~1), CL = FALSE, detectfn = 0, method = "Newton-Raphson", mask=mask)

metapop.fit

Then I tried the same code, but made a change to the secr.fit argument following p. 6 of secr-multisession.pdf, with the following change to the code starting on the secr.fit line:

library(MASS)
metapop.fit <- secr.fit (CHmetapop, model = D~session, CL = FALSE, detectfn = 0, method = "Newton-Raphson", mask=mask, details=list(contrasts=list(session=MASS::contr.sdif)))

coef(metapop.fit)

beta <- coef(metapop.fit)[2:3, 'beta']
sebeta <- coef(metapop.fit)[2:3, 'SE.beta']
exp(beta)

exp(beta)*sqrt(exp(sebeta^2)-1)
D<-collate(metapop.fit, realnames='D')[,1,1,]
D[2:3]/D[1:2]

I got the error on the collate step "Warning message:
In collate(metapop.fit, realnames = "D") : only one model"

So it seems I am having an issue getting secr to recognize that I want estimates for each year separately, and also for the two years combined. Any suggestions on achieving both yearly estimates and a combined estimate for the two years would be greatly appreciated.

Best,
Melissa

messages.body_plain:
Hi Luciano

I think you are expecting too much of 'secr' and your data. You have only one animal with telemetry data and that was not detected at a camera - how can that individual represent the behaviour of the whole population? As usual, I am averse to combining capture-recapture and telemetry. You are free to play 'what if...' games by estimating sigma from the telemetry data and fixing sigma to that value in the capture-recapture analysis; that keeps the logic clean, but I wouldn't get excited about the result.

'secr' does not model detection as a function of landscape (mask) covariates (but you can associate covariates with detectors). It seems that your covariates have a large number of levels (indicated by " c,m,t combinations  exceed..."), which demands a lot of memory in 'secr'. You could try collapsing those covariates into fewer discrete values.

I think you have 32 detections of 10 animals, and that is at the lower limit of what is required for any (spatial) capture-recapture model. I doubt there is power to distinguish among more fancy models, so I wouldn't go there.

Of course, others may see this differently.

Murray

The output from predictDsurface is a Dsurface object, a special sort of mask with its own plot method. Check ?predictDsurface and its examples.
surfaces <- predictDsurface(V3PropDensU.fit)
par(mfrow = c(2,1))
plot(surfaces)

mean(covariates(surfaces[[1]])$D.0)  # average predicted density over mask 1
